title: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
summary: Generate several phrasings of a question with an LLM, retrieve each in parallel, and merge by union or RRF. See how N moves recall, latency and cost, and when drift or rerank budgets erase the gain.
outcomes: Explain why one phrasing of a query misses relevant documents and how multiple phrasings raise first-stage recall
Trace the generate, parallel retrieve and merge stages, including LangChain and LlamaIndex defaults
Compute fused RRF rankings and recall@k for a set of per-query lists, and choose union or RRF and a dedup key
Estimate how N affects recall, latency and retriever load with parallel searches
Recognize drift, redundant paraphrases and rerank budgets, and decide when to skip multi-query or decompose instead

lessons.title: Why one phrasing of a question misses relevant documents

blocks.md: A retriever answers the query it is given, not the need behind it. Dense retrieval embeds the query string into one vector and returns its nearest neighbors; BM25 matches its exact terms. Change a few words and you land in a different neighborhood of the index, even though the person wants the same thing.

This is not a rare edge case. In the UQV100 collection, crowd workers were each given a short backstory for one of 100 TREC Web Track topics and asked to write the query they would type. They produced **10,835** query variations for those 100 topics (as described by Benham et al.). Penha, Camara and Hauff built a taxonomy of the rewrites seen in UQV100 (such as paraphrases, word order changes and more natural phrasing; they added misspellings because UQV100 had been spell-corrected), generated such variations automatically for TREC-DL-2019 and ANTIQUE queries, and found retrieval pipelines lost about **20%** effectiveness on average under variations that keep the meaning.

The idea of using several phrasings is old. Benham et al. recount that Belkin and colleagues had experienced searchers write several Boolean queries for the same topics and combined their outputs by summing retrieval scores, and that fusing query variations has repeatedly been found to raise effectiveness. **Multi-query retrieval** is the LLM-era version: instead of asking several humans, ask a language model for several phrasings, retrieve with each, and merge the results.

blocks.title: Toy corpus: one question, five relevant documents

scenes.caption: Our running example. The question has five relevant documents: d1, d3, d5, d7 and d8. Everything else in the index (d2, d4, d6, d9 to d15) is not relevant.
The user's own phrasing, q0, returns d1, d2, d4, d3, d6. Two of its five results are relevant, so recall@5 = 2/5 = 0.4.
d5, d7 and d8 are missing. They are relevant but written in words this phrasing does not reach, so no amount of reranking q0's list can surface them.

blocks.caption: Recall@k: the share of all relevant documents that appear in the first k results. For q0: 2 of 5, so 0.4.

blocks.prompt: Suppose you rerank q0's five results with a perfect cross-encoder that always puts relevant documents first. What is recall@5 afterwards?
blocks.reveal: Still **0.4**. A reranker only reorders the candidates it is given. d5, d7 and d8 were never retrieved, so they cannot come back. Recall is decided at the first stage, which is why techniques that widen the candidate set (hybrid search, query expansion, multi-query) exist at all.

blocks.title: Recall@5 of four phrasings of the same need

scenes.caption: Only the original query, at 0.4.
Three LLM-generated phrasings retrieve their own top-5 lists. q1 and q2 each reach 0.6, beating the user's wording. q3 drifted to a different topic and scores 0.
No single phrasing is best for every relevant document, and one is useless. Multi-query retrieval bets that the union of several phrasings covers more than any one of them.

blocks.md: Multi-query is not a magic recall knob. In our toy no phrasing ever retrieves d8, so even the full union of all lists tops out at recall 0.8. Multi-query can only find documents that some phrasing ranks within the per-query depth.

Retrieval quality depends on the exact words of the query. Multi-query retrieval treats the user's wording as one sample from many possible phrasings and retrieves with several samples instead of betting on one.

blocks.question: A team adds a strong cross-encoder reranker on top of single-query dense retrieval (top-20), and recall@20 does not change. Why?
options: The reranker needs a larger k constant
A reranker reorders candidates but cannot add documents the first stage never returned
Cross-encoders ignore the query wording
Recall@20 always equals precision@20
blocks.explain: Recall@20 counts relevant documents among the 20 candidates. Reordering those 20 cannot change which documents are in the set. Raising first-stage recall needs a different candidate generator, such as more phrasings, BM25 or a larger depth.

lessons.title: The multi-query pipeline: generate, retrieve in parallel, merge

blocks.md: The pattern has three stages. **Generate**: one LLM call turns the question into N alternative phrasings (paraphrases or perspectives on the same need). **Retrieve**: run every phrasing against the same retriever, concurrently. **Merge**: combine the N ranked lists into one, removing duplicates. From the query-rewriting course you know how to prompt for rewrites; here the point is that we keep *several* rewrites and use them all.

scenes.caption: Baseline RAG: the question goes straight to the retriever as a single query and its top-k list is the context.
Stage 1: one LLM call writes N alternative phrasings. This call is on the critical path: no generated query can be searched until it returns.
Stage 2: every query, often including the original, is searched independently. These calls do not depend on each other, so they can run at the same time.
Stage 3: the lists are merged. A deduplicated union keeps every distinct document; RRF also orders them by how strongly the lists agree. Then the result is cut to k.

blocks.md:
Three widely used implementations differ in small but important defaults, all visible in their source:

- **LangChain `MultiQueryRetriever`**: the default prompt asks for 3 different versions of the question, parsed one per line; every non-empty line becomes a query, with no cap at 3. `include_original` defaults to `False`, so only the 3 rewrites are searched. The result is the **unique union** of all retrieved documents, with no fusion scoring.
- **LlamaIndex `QueryFusionRetriever`**: `num_queries=4` by default, and that count **includes** the original, so the LLM is asked for 3. `mode` selects the merge: `simple` (the default, keep each node's max score), `reciprocal_rerank` (RRF), `relative_score` or `dist_based_score`. The merged list is cut to `similarity_top_k`.
- **RAG-Fusion** (Raudaschl's reference repo): asks for 4 queries, searches them **plus** the original, and fuses with RRF using k = 60.

blocks.code:
from langchain_classic.retrievers.multi_query import MultiQueryRetriever

mq = MultiQueryRetriever.from_llm(
    retriever=vectorstore.as_retriever(search_kwargs={"k": 5}),
    llm=llm,
    include_original=True,   # default False: only the rewrites are searched
)
docs = mq.invoke("how do I stop my laptop overheating")
# docs = unique union of up to 4 x 5 documents, in query order, not ranked
blocks.caption: LangChain's retriever wraps any base retriever. The async path (ainvoke) searches all queries with asyncio.gather; the sync path loops over them one at a time.

blocks.md: LangChain's synchronous `invoke` searches the generated queries **one after another** in a for loop; only the async `ainvoke` path runs them concurrently with `asyncio.gather`. LlamaIndex runs them concurrently when `use_async=True` (its default). If your multi-query latency grows linearly with N, check which path you are on.

Below is a minimal end-to-end version with the three stages written out: one LLM call, concurrent searches, then RRF over document ids. Step through it on our toy, where the LLM returns q1, q2, q3 and every search returns a top-5 list (all four lists are shown in full in the next lesson).

blocks.title: A minimal multi-query retriever, traced on the toy
blocks.code:
import asyncio

async def multi_query(question, llm, search, n=3, k=60, top=5):
    variants = await llm.paraphrase(question, n)
    seen = dict.fromkeys(v.strip().lower() for v in variants if v.strip())
    queries = [question] + [q for q in seen if q != question.lower()]
    lists = await asyncio.gather(*(search(q, top) for q in queries))
    scores = {}
    for hits in lists:
        for rank, doc_id in enumerate(hits, start=1):
            scores[doc_id] = scores.get(doc_id, 0.0) + 1 / (k + rank)
    fused = sorted(scores, key=scores.get, reverse=True)
    return fused[:top]

scenes.caption: One LLM call returns three phrasings. Nothing else can start until it finishes.
Normalize and drop empty or exact-duplicate rewrites (and any copy of the original), then put the original first. Cheap insurance against wasted searches.
All four searches are awaited together, so wall time is set by the slowest search, not the sum.
Each appearance adds 1/(k + rank). d3 appears in three lists (ranks 4, 1, 2), so it accumulates the most.
Sort by fused score, keep the top 5. The dictionary keyed by doc_id already removed duplicates.

blocks.md: Keep the original query in the set unless you have a reason not to. It is the only phrasing guaranteed not to drift, and it costs one extra search, not an extra LLM call. RAG-Fusion and LlamaIndex include it by default; LangChain makes it opt-in.

blocks.question: You configure LlamaIndex `QueryFusionRetriever(num_queries=4, ...)` with one retriever. How many LLM-generated queries and how many searches does one call make?
options: 4 generated, 4 searches
4 generated, 5 searches
3 generated, 4 searches
1 generated, 4 searches
blocks.explain: num_queries counts the original. The prompt asks the LLM for num_queries - 1 = 3 queries, and the original plus those 3 are each searched once per retriever: 4 searches. Setting num_queries=1 disables generation.

blocks.question: A LangChain `MultiQueryRetriever` with defaults is called through `invoke` over a base retriever with k = 5. What comes back?
options: The 5 highest RRF-scored documents
Up to 15 unique documents from the 3 rewrites, in the order they were retrieved
Exactly 20 documents including duplicates
Only the documents that appear in all 3 lists
blocks.explain: With include_original=False, 3 rewrites are searched (sequentially on the sync path) and the unique union is returned, up to 3 x 5 = 15 documents, in query order. There is no rank fusion and no truncation to k.

lessons.title: Union versus RRF, and deduplicating by document id

blocks.md: Once you have N lists you must decide what the downstream step receives. A **deduplicated union** passes every distinct document. **Fusion** (here RRF, from the prereq course: each list adds $1/(k + r)$ for a document at rank r, with k = 60) produces one ranked list that can be cut to the same k as a single query. The two give very different context sizes and orders.

blocks.title: Four top-5 lists for the same question

scenes.caption: Each query's top-5 list, relevant documents in green. 20 slots in total.
Duplicates: d3 appears in q0, q1 and q2; d1, d5, d2 and d9 each appear twice. A union removes 6 repeats and keeps 14 distinct documents.
Union recall: d1, d3, d5 and d7 are all somewhere in the 14 documents, so recall over the union is 4/5 = 0.8. The price is a context of 14 documents instead of 5, 10 of them not relevant.

blocks.md: RRF with k = 60 and ranks counted from 1 gives the scores below (computed by script). Documents found by several phrasings rise; a document found by only one phrasing, even at rank 1, scores at most $1/61 \approx 0.01639$. Note: LlamaIndex and the RAG-Fusion repo count ranks from 0, so their rank-1 term is $1/60$ and every score shifts slightly.

blocks.title: RRF scores over q0 to q3 (k = 60)

scenes.caption: d3 is in three lists (ranks 4, 1, 2): 1/64 + 1/61 + 1/62 = 0.04815, a clear winner.
d1 (ranks 1, 3), d5 (2, 4), d2 (2, 5) and d9 (4, 3) each appear twice and land between 0.0315 and 0.0323.
d7 is rank 1 for q2 only: 0.01639, tied with d12, the rank-1 result of the drifted q3. Fused top-5 is d3, d1, d5, d2, d9: recall@5 = 3/5 = 0.6, up from 0.4.

blocks.prompt: Drop the drifted query q3 and fuse only q0, q1, q2. What happens to fused recall@5?
blocks.reveal: It rises to **0.8**. Without q3, d9 appears only once (rank 4 in q1, 0.01563), so it falls below d7 (0.01639). The fused top-5 becomes d3, d1, d5, d2, d7. One off-topic phrasing cost a relevant document, while using one fewer search. More queries is not automatically better.

blocks.title: Recall@5 for each way of using the lists

scenes.caption: Single query: 0.4 with 5 documents.
Adding one good paraphrase lifts fused recall@5 to 0.6. All four lists also give 0.6.
Without the drifted query, 0.8 at the same 5-document budget. The union also covers 0.8 but needs 14 documents, so it is not comparable at k = 5.

blocks.md: **Deduplication** decides what counts as the same document, and the libraries differ. LangChain's `unique_union` keeps a document unless an *equal* `Document` object came before it, and `Document` equality compares all of its fields (text, metadata, id). LlamaIndex keys its fusion dictionaries by `node.hash`, which for a text node is a SHA-256 hash of its text plus metadata. Neither knows that two different chunks come from the same source page.

For RRF the key choice changes the scores themselves. Keying by **chunk id** lets two chunks of one page each take a slot. Keying by **source document id** merges them, so the page collects every phrasing's vote, and you then pick which chunk to show. Choose the key on purpose, use a stable id from your index rather than object equality, and dedup *before* truncating to k, otherwise repeats waste context slots.

Union and RRF are not interchangeable. A union returns everything (N x k documents at worst) in retrieval order, so taking its first k usually just returns the first query's list. Pick RRF when the next stage has a fixed budget; pick union when a reranker will score all candidates anyway.

RRF rewards agreement between phrasings. A relevant document that only one phrasing finds stays low, and a junk document that two phrasings share can outrank it. That is why the quality of the phrasings matters as much as their number.

blocks.question: Your index stores 3 chunks per web page. Fusion is keyed by chunk id and the top-5 after RRF holds 3 chunks of the same page. What is the most direct fix?
options: Fuse by source document id (or collapse chunks of one page) before truncating to 5
Raise k from 60 to 600
Generate more paraphrases
Switch from RRF to an unranked union
blocks.explain: The slots are being spent on near-duplicates of one source. Keying fusion or a post-fusion collapse by source id frees slots for other documents. Changing k or adding phrasings does not address what counts as a duplicate.

blocks.question: In the toy, why does d2 (not relevant) outrank d7 (relevant) after fusing all four lists?
options: d2 has a higher cosine similarity
d2 appears in two lists while d7 appears in only one, and RRF sums contributions
RRF gives rank 1 a weight of zero
d7 was removed by deduplication
blocks.explain: RRF adds one term per list. d2 gets 1/62 + 1/65 = 0.03151; d7 gets only 1/61 = 0.01639 even though it was ranked first by q2. Agreement beats a single strong vote.

lessons.title: How N trades recall against latency and cost

blocks.md: Each extra phrasing costs one more embedding and one more search, and adds candidates the next stage has to read. What it buys depends on how *different* the phrasing is. A paraphrase that retrieves the same list adds nothing; one that reaches a new region adds documents. Here is a simplified model to build intuition (not a measured law): the first query finds each relevant document with probability p, and each extra phrasing finds a still-missing one with probability $p(1-\rho)$, where $\rho$ is how correlated the phrasings are.

blocks.caption: Simplified model. With p = 0.4: independent phrasings (rho = 0) give 0.64 at N = 2 and 0.87 at N = 4; highly correlated ones (rho = 0.8) give 0.448 and 0.533.

blocks.title: Union recall vs number of queries (simplified model)

scenes.caption: p = 0.4, rho = 0.5: recall rises from 0.4 to 0.69 at N = 4 and 0.80 at N = 6. Each extra query adds less than the one before.
rho = 0.8 models redundant paraphrases: 0.53 at N = 4. You pay four searches for a small gain.
rho = 0: truly different phrasings, 0.87 at N = 4. Diversity, not count, drives the curve. Real phrasings also drift, which this model ignores.

blocks.md: Latency has a different shape. The LLM call comes first and is usually the largest fixed cost. After it, if the searches run concurrently, the wait is set by the **slowest** of the N searches. Benham et al. describe exactly this for parallel fusion of query variations: each query's latency is dictated by the slowest-running variation, and the speed comes at a resource cost because every variation still consumes CPU.

blocks.title: One request, under a stated latency model

scenes.caption: Assumed numbers, for illustration: embed 20 ms, search 40 ms. A single query finishes at 60 ms.
Multi-query, sequential: LLM 600 ms, batched embed 25 ms, then searches of 40, 45, 50 and 90 ms one after another, fuse 1 ms. Total 851 ms.
Parallel searches: the four start together and fusion waits for the slowest (90 ms). Total 716 ms. The LLM call is now 84% of the request.
A straggler: q3's search takes 300 ms (a cold cache, say). Everyone waits: 926 ms. More parallel calls means more chances that one of them is slow.
A 100 ms deadline on the search phase: q3 is abandoned and the three lists that returned are fused. Total 726 ms, at the cost of whatever q3 would have contributed.

blocks.md: How fast does the slowest-of-N grow? If each search time were exponentially distributed with mean m, the expected maximum of N of them is $m H_N$, where $H_N = 1 + 1/2 + \dots + 1/N$ is the harmonic number. With m = 40 ms that is 40, 60, 73 and 83 ms for N = 1 to 4. Sequential search grows as $mN$ instead: 40, 80, 120, 160 ms.

blocks.title: Retrieval phase time vs N (exponential search times)

scenes.caption: m = 40 ms. At N = 4 sequential needs 160 ms, parallel about 83 ms (the curve uses the standard approximation of H_N, within 3 ms of the exact value here).
m = 80 ms. The parallel curve still grows slowly with N, but each search also uses a CPU or GPU slot, so total retriever load grows as N, not log N.

blocks.md: Cost, per request: 1 LLM call (prompt plus N short outputs), N query embeddings, N searches, and a larger context if you pass a union to the generator. In Rackauckas's RAG-Fusion study at Infineon, ten back-to-back runs averaged 34.62 s against 19.52 s for plain RAG, 1.77 times slower. The author attributes most of the difference to the *final* answer call, which now reads more queries and documents; the query-generation call never took more than 5 s in those runs.

Practical knobs: generate all phrasings in **one** LLM call, embed them in one batch, search concurrently with a deadline, and pass a fused top-k (not the raw union) to the generator. Rackauckas suggests generating fewer queries and lowering LLM latency as the main ways to cut time.

blocks.question: Searches run in parallel and the LLM rewrite takes 600 ms. You raise N from 4 to 8. Which effect is largest, under the model in this lesson?
options: End-to-end latency roughly doubles
Latency and load both stay the same
Recall doubles
End-to-end latency rises a little, while retriever load and candidate count roughly double
blocks.explain: In parallel, the search phase grows with the slowest of N (about m H_N: 83 ms to 109 ms at m = 40), small next to 600 ms of LLM time. But every extra query is another search to serve and more candidates downstream, so load and context grow linearly. Recall gains shrink as N grows.

blocks.question: Using the simplified model with p = 0.4, which change helps recall more at N = 4: making phrasings less similar (rho from 0.8 to 0.5) or adding four more similar phrasings (N = 8 at rho = 0.8)?
options: Adding four more similar phrasings
Both give exactly the same recall
Making phrasings less similar
Neither changes recall
blocks.explain: At rho = 0.5, N = 4 gives 0.693. At rho = 0.8, N = 8 gives 0.665, with twice the searches. Diverse phrasings beat more of the same.

lessons.title: Drift, redundancy, reranker budgets, and when to skip it

blocks.md: **Query drift**: a generated phrasing that answers a different question. Rackauckas reports that RAG-Fusion answers were accurate and comprehensive, but some strayed off topic when the generated queries were not relevant enough to the original. An example from the paper: asking whether a microphone is good for an outdoor surveillance camera led the LLM to write queries treating the microphone as a camera itself, until the question was reworded. In our toy, q3 drifted and its rank-1 junk document tied the relevant d7.

**Redundant paraphrases**: phrasings that differ in words but retrieve the same list. They add searches and, under RRF, double-count the same opinion. If the LLM returns a phrasing whose top-5 equals q0's, fusing the two simply doubles every score: the order and recall (0.4) are unchanged, and you paid for a second search.

blocks.title: Overlap (Jaccard) between the toy top-5 lists

scenes.caption: Jaccard overlap = shared documents / distinct documents across two lists. q0 and q1 share 3 of 7 (0.429): q1 adds two new documents, d5 and d9.
q2 barely overlaps q0 (0.111) and brings d7, a new relevant document. Low overlap with useful results is what you want.
q3 has zero overlap with q0 and q2. Zero overlap is also the signature of drift: low overlap alone cannot tell a new angle from a wrong topic.

blocks.md: Asking for diversity cuts both ways. Raudaschl's repo has a diverse mode whose prompt asks for synonyms, broader or narrower framings and related sub-topics, and to avoid minor rewordings. That reduces redundancy but pushes phrasings toward the edge of the topic, where drift lives. Inspect generated queries on real traffic before tuning N.

**Recall gains that do not survive the rest of the pipeline.** A 2026 study of fusion in an enterprise RAG deployment (115 support queries, retrieval depth fixed at 10, cross-encoder reranking and truncation) found that multi-query fusion did raise raw recall, but after reranking and truncation the gains were largely neutralized: fusion did not beat the single-query baseline on KB-level top-k accuracy, with Hit@10 falling from 0.51 to 0.48 in several configurations, while adding latency.

blocks.prompt: Why could higher first-stage recall fail to improve the final top-10 after a reranker?
blocks.reveal: The reranker sees a fixed budget of candidates and the generator a fixed context. If fusion adds relevant documents near the bottom of the pool, or crowds it with near-duplicates and off-topic hits, the reranker can still pick the same top 10 as before, or a worse one. The recall gain is real at depth N x k but does not reach the depth that matters.

blocks.md: **Not the same as decomposition.** Multi-query asks the *same* question several ways and runs the phrasings independently. Decomposition splits a *compound* question into different sub-questions. LlamaIndex's `SubQuestionQueryEngine` breaks a complex query into sub-questions for each relevant data source, answers each, then synthesizes a final answer. Self-Ask (Press et al.) has the model ask and answer follow-up questions before the final answer, so later steps can depend on earlier answers. Paraphrasing a two-hop question four times does not answer either hop.

blocks.title: Should this query use multi-query retrieval?

nodes.label:
exact id, code,
or known item?

scenes.caption: Identifiers, error codes and exact titles are precision problems. Paraphrasing them only adds noise; lexical or hybrid search on the original is the right tool.
Compound or multi-hop questions need different sub-questions, not more phrasings of the whole. Use decomposition.
Vague queries or vocabulary mismatch with the corpus are the target. If the extra LLM call breaks the latency budget, skip it; otherwise multi-query plus RRF.

blocks.md: Use multi-query when recall is the bottleneck because users word things differently from the corpus, and the next stage can absorb more candidates. Skip it for precise lookups, compound questions (decompose instead), tight latency budgets, and pipelines where a fixed reranker budget already decides the outcome. Measure end-to-end, not just first-stage recall.

blocks.question: Users ask: "Which of our two vendors had more outages last quarter, and what did each change afterwards?" Retrieval misses half the evidence. What is the best fit?
options: Decompose into sub-questions (outages per vendor, changes per vendor) and retrieve for each
Multi-query with 6 paraphrases and RRF
Raise the RRF constant k
Use the unique union instead of RRF
blocks.explain: The question has several distinct parts. Paraphrases of the whole question keep mixing them; sub-questions target each needed fact, in the spirit of SubQuestionQueryEngine or Self-Ask.

blocks.question: After enabling multi-query, recall@50 of the candidate pool rises from 0.62 to 0.78, but answer accuracy is flat. The reranker keeps the top 10. What should you check first?
options: Whether the newly found relevant documents make it into the reranker's top 10
Whether k = 60 is too small
Whether the LLM is generating exactly 3 queries
Whether the vector index uses cosine or dot product
blocks.explain: This is the pattern the enterprise study reports: first-stage gains neutralized by a fixed rerank and truncation budget. Measure recall at the depth the generator actually sees before tuning anything upstream.

blocks.question: The LLM sometimes returns phrasings that shift the question to a neighboring topic. Which change most directly limits the damage?
options: Raise N so the drifted phrasing is outvoted
Keep the original query in the set and inspect or filter generated queries that look off-topic
Replace RRF with an unranked union
Drop the original query to avoid bias
blocks.explain: The original query cannot drift and anchors fusion. Filtering clearly off-topic rewrites (or constraining the prompt) removes the junk list. Raising N adds cost and may add more drift; a union passes drifted results straight through.
